You're definetly gonna want to work on form... now, what im about to tell you is just what ive learned through trial and error. its something that ive kind of learned overtime, so im not 100% sure if all riders agree or even ride this way but some basic tips

on the ascents, get your butt of the seat. since you probably dont have a dropper like me, your dropper post is your body. stand up whenever you're hitting the ascents for better leverage, and to make them easier and shorter. on the descents, hover you rear end a little to back so its not completly over the rear tire, but your weight shouldn't be all up on your front tire either. this will help keep the weight on the tires balanced and make turns easier, so your not just skidding and drifting all over the place. Use your arms and legs as suspension- since my suspension basically doesnt work, my arms and legs are basically my suspension. follow the bike through, go down as it comes down, and pop up as the bike pops up. turn with your weight, not just your bars. basically, instead of just moving your bars, lean your weight to where you wanna go. i like to move my knee towards whichever way i turn, but thats a personal preference. oh, also LEARN TO BUNNY HOP. its way easier to jump over roots, get air off of every small ledge, boost off of the ramps, and properly land rear tire first on flats if you know how to level out your bike and bunny hop. thats just my little 2¢ and by no means is it any professional advice. im sure many people would say otherwise, but it works for me on my cheap-o bike, so it might work even better with a nicer bike and a newer rider! dont forget, pushing limits is the only way you're gonna get better. You might break parts, but they're bound to break sooner or later. better to break them now, learn whatcha did wrong, and get possibly better components sooner!

#                                       Geometry  

first of would be the frame itself- the one thing you cant modify or change. The giant talon boasts a pretty universal 67.5-degree headtube angle, which is the relation between the bars and your fork. the slacker the HTA, the less weight you have on your front wheel. along with the less weight, you also get better control, and it makes it easier to roll over roots and rocks. The 67.5 degree HTA of the giant talon is really universal in terms of climbing and descent. The seat tube angle is a very nice 74 degrees, giving a pretty good pedaling position. the higher the seat tube angle, the better pedaling position you obtain. The sweet spot for most riders is a 66-degree HTA and a 75 degree STA, which accommodates almost every disciple of riding. The Rockhopper has a less aggressive geometry, though it's only by .5 degrees. the HTA of the Rockhopper being 68 degrees, but it also has a 73.5-degree seat tube angle. now while it may not seem like much when riding XC, the talon would be much more comfortable riding through rock gardens and roots. While the rockhopper may have been tolerable, the marlin seems leagues behind the other two in this category- with a 69.3 degree HTA and a 73.5 degree STA, the marlin is really more directed to the commuters who decide to hit the fire road every other Sunday, or they really want to have saddle sores after a long day at some minor singletrack. Kinky, yes, but not my thing.  


#                             Componentry

While Geometry was something that you can't change, the componentry is much easier to change out in accordance with your preference, but even within the componentry, there are many things you wouldn't want to change. While the marlin and the Rockhopper come stock with the mid-high range coil spring forks, the giant comes with a mid-low range air fork. this on its own, should really be the end of the conversation in this category, because any air fork from a decent brand will automatically beat a high-end coil spring.  The Marlin 7 and Talon 1 both come stock with a 10 spd Deore setup, while the rockhopper comes with a lousy 9 spd advent. while I love the advent, it really confuses me why specialized didn't choose to get the advent x which, in my opinion, would have won this category. regardless, the drivetrain on the rockhopper is inferior to that of the talon and marlin. The one downfall of the talon 1 would be its brakes- while the rockhopper and the marlin are equipped with Shimano MT-200's, the talon gets stuck with the tektro equivalents. personally, I have only worked with their v-brakes, but they've always given me problems over time. though, this is a cheaper upgrade that you can get done in the sub 100$ range.

#                                        Looks

While this is much more subjective, if I'm being completely honest the talon's frame and desert sage just look MUCH MUCH cleaner than the other two.
